explain.say: The salt on your table may once have been part of the sea! Look at the first stage. Along sunny coasts, seawater is let into huge, flat, shallow pools called salt pans. Every litre of seawater holds about 35 grams of salt.

faq.q: Why are salt pans so shallow?
faq.a: Shallow water warms up quickly and has a big surface for the Sun and wind to dry, so the water evaporates much faster.
Water can hold only so much dissolved salt. As it evaporates, the extra salt comes out as solid crystals, and because salt particles stack in a cube pattern, the crystals are tiny cubes.
asks: Why is salt shaped like cubes?

faq.q: How much salt is in seawater?
faq.a: About 35 grams in every litre, or roughly 3.5 percent. Most of it is sodium chloride, the same salt you eat.
In sunny, dry coastal places, such as Gujarat in India, Guérande in France, Guerrero Negro in Mexico and many coasts of China.

faq.q: Is all salt from the sea?
faq.a: No. A lot of salt is mined from underground rock salt, which formed when ancient seas dried up millions of years ago.

facts: Average seawater contains about 35 grams of dissolved salts per litre.
Gujarat produces most of India's salt, largely by solar evaporation of seawater and brine.
